title: Cahokia, City of Mounds
objective: After this level you can describe Cahokia, the Mississippian city near today's St. Louis, and what its great mounds were for.
summary: Cahokia, near St. Louis, was the largest city north of Mexico (about 950 to 1350), perhaps bigger than London around 1100. Its earthen mounds, led by Monks Mound, held its seat of power.

cards.headline: Around 1100, a city of dirt near St. Louis probably outnumbered London.
cards.body: Not stone, not brick: earth, carried in baskets and piled into hills. Welcome to Cahokia.

cards.headline: The biggest city north of Mexico
cards.body: Cahokia, near present-day St. Louis, was the largest urban center north of Mexico, and it flourished from about 950 to 1350. Most of its people were farmers, and corn was the center of their farming. At its peak, around 1100, it may have held 15,000 to 20,000 people, probably a little more than London at the time. A visiting Londoner would have been the country cousin.

cards.headline: A hill made by hand
cards.body: Cahokia’s mounds were built of earth carried to the site basket by basket. The biggest, Monks Mound, rises about 100 feet, and its base is about the size of the Great Pyramid of Giza’s. It is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. On top once stood a building about 100 feet long, believed to be the seat of Cahokia’s government. City hall, on a hill its people made.
cards.callout: Monks Mound: about 100 feet tall, built of earth

mascot.line: If you remember one thing, make it this: Cahokia’s biggest mound was a platform for power, built by hand.

cards.headline: A calendar made of posts
cards.body: Cahokians also set up circles of wooden posts, now called Woodhenge. At certain times of the year the rising sun lined up with the posts, so the circles served as a calendar. No batteries, no paper, and it never ran slow.

cards.headline: Why did it empty out?
cards.body: By about 1350, Cahokia’s great days were over. The likeliest cause is environmental damage: cutting the forests brought erosion and flooding. Disease, climate change, social stress and warfare may also have played a part. Nobody left a note, so historians weigh the clues.

Its decline most likely came from environmental damage
